defuser_messages.message: Front face: only one interactive module visible, top-left. It’s a square panel with 6 wires running left-to-right. Wire colors from top to bottom: 1) yellow, 2) white, 3) red, 4) yellow, 5) red, 6) black. Timer reads 01:17. I see no red strike Xs above the timer.
I cut the 2nd (white) wire and got a strike: there is now 1 red X above the timer. Timer now shows 01:07. Wire module not solved (status light not green). What next wire should I cut?
Confirming wires top to bottom as seen now: 1) yellow, 2) white (this one is cut), 3) red, 4) yellow, 5) red, 6) black.
Right side: I see one port, a Serial port (9-pin D-sub). No batteries, no indicator lights, no serial number on this side.
Back face has no modules visible (just blank panels). Bottom edge: one labelled indicator light reading "BOB"; the light itself is unlit. No batteries, no serial number, no other ports visible here.
Left side: serial number label reads N0XKL3 (with a zero after N). One labelled indicator light above it reads "TRN" and it is lit white. No batteries and no ports on this side.

All 6 wires appear solid single colors, no stripes/two-tone. From top to bottom: 1) solid yellow, uncut. 2) solid white, cut. 3) solid red, uncut. 4) solid yellow, uncut. 5) solid red, uncut. 6) solid black, uncut.

1) Outcome: the bomb exploded due to time running out. I contributed by quickly reporting the visible 6-wire setup and later gathering edgework (serial, indicators, port). You contributed by giving a cut instruction and then requesting verification/edgework to resolve the unexpected strike. We didn’t converge on a correct next action before time expired.
2) Communication challenges: the biggest mismatch was that the wire-cut instruction should have been correct for the described colors, yet it produced a strike. That created uncertainty about whether my wire-color report was wrong, whether the module wasn’t actually a standard 6-wire puzzle, or whether we were referencing different rule conditions. The back-and-forth verification plus edgework collection consumed time and stalled progress.
3) Mistakes/missed opportunities: (a) Cutting the 2nd wire led to an immediate strike (clear feedback: 1 red X appeared and module LED stayed unsolved). After that, we spent too long reconciling instead of moving to other solvable modules (if any) or re-checking for other modules. (b) I initially didn’t proactively provide full edgework (serial/batteries/indicators/ports) before the first cut; if the module had required it, that delayed us. (c) I also should have re-checked whether there were other modules on other faces earlier; we later found the back face appeared empty, but that was only after time was already lower. These could be avoided by doing a fast “edgework sweep” and “module inventory” at the start, then solving.
4) What worked well: concise reporting of exact wire order and later providing serial number (N0XKL3), indicators (TRN lit, BOB unlit), and a Serial port. What didn’t work: committing to a cut before we had high confidence, and then getting stuck in diagnosis mode rather than switching tasks.
5) Changes next time: do a 10–15 second initial scan: count modules on front/back, then immediately collect serial number, batteries, indicators, and ports before any risky action. After any unexpected strike, pause cutting and either (a) move to a different module, or (b) re-verify the module type by describing all features (wire count, presence/absence of star/LED, any text) to ensure we’re using the right manual section.
6) Lessons: early shared context (edgework + full module inventory) prevents later rework; after a strike, treat it as evidence of a wrong assumption and pivot quickly; and when something contradicts the manual, the fastest recovery is to re-describe the entire module visually to confirm we’re solving the correct puzzle, rather than repeatedly validating a single detail.
